## Keep or rush

In class order. Planned total about 75 of the 80 minutes.

| Item | Min | | If short |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Discussion 1: Absurd Trolley Problems, and which framework each side of a disagreement used | 10 | Rush | Play for four minutes; one disagreement from the room |
| Discussion 2: the arguments they brought: whose good counts, the graph, a rival graph, and an argument against the policy that accepts its causal claims | 12 | Keep | Two groups' graphs on the screen instead of every group's |
| Problem 1: conditioning and intervening, with feedback | 11 | Keep | Work (b) to (d) together; say (e): nothing points into $X$, so observing $X$ and setting it agree |
| Problem 2: adjusting for a confounder, with feedback | 12 | Keep | (a) and (b) only; give (d), 0.18 |
| Discussion 3: what the Belmont--Menlo principles or the five Cs require of a model that decides about people | 13 | Rush | Show the GP example and ask each group for one requirement it would add |
| Discussion 4: four parts of the room make the case for one framework each, then the vote | 13 | Keep | Three minutes to prepare, one sentence from each part, then the vote |
| To finish, and the task for next time | 4 | Keep | Read the task aloud |

: {tbl-colwidths="[32,6,16,46]"}

Minimum class, about 45 minutes: discussion 2, problems 1 and 2, discussion 4 in its short form and the task for next time. With more time, add discussion 3 back first.

## If you read on

How it runs

- Students bring one argument from the news that justifies a rule or a policy by its consequences, with the cause-and-effect claims it needs. Open the [complete class sheet](https://ethics4ds.com/teachers/wk03/class_complete.html) on screen: green boxes are hints, opened in order after a few minutes; blue boxes are answers.
- Discussion 1 needs one phone or laptop per group for [Absurd Trolley Problems](https://neal.fun/absurd-trolley-problems/). Groups will not finish the game; stop them at six minutes.
- Discussion 3: give half the groups the Belmont--Menlo principles and half the five Cs.
- Discussion 4: split the room into four parts by where people sit, and keep to five minutes of preparation and a minute each. Everyone votes for the account they find most convincing, which need not be the one they argued for; count hands or use a poll.
- Problem 2(c) to (e) was not in the lecture: effects that differ between rows, so the average treatment effect depends on the population's mix, and a decision is compared with today, not with nobody treated. Both are in the notes, under "For the class".
- Everything headed "Optional, can be done at home" is outside the class, including the R simulation (coding C).

What students should see

- Problem 1: $P(W = 1) = 0.4$ and $P(X = 0 \mid W = 1) = 0.75$; $P(H = 1 \mid W = 1) = 0.325$ against $P(H = 1 \mid W = 0) = 0.2$; $P(H = 1 \mid do(W := 0)) = 0.25$; the average treatment effect of exercise is $-0.3$.
- Problem 2: 0.74 against 0.38 observed; 0.65 against 0.50 adjusted, an effect of 0.15; 0.10 and 0.20 within the rows; 0.18 in the second school. For (e), 0.56 today against 0.65 if every student used the app; among today's non-users the effect is 0.18, the same as (d) because they have the second school's mix.
- Discussion 3: requirements stated as mechanisms (an opt-out, an audit by group, a data-retention rule), and the distinction between accuracy and the effect of using the model.

Where they get stuck

- Discussion 2, question 4: arguing about the causal claims again. Ask them to grant every claim and object anyway.
- Problem 1(c): forgetting that $W = 1$ also happens with exercise, at rate 0.2, or not conditioning on $X$ before treating $W$ and $H$ as independent.
- Problem 2(b): weighting each row by its share of users, which gives back 0.74, instead of its share of all students.
- Calling the 28 points "biased" without saying of what. As a description of attenders against non-attenders it is correct; as an estimate of the effect it is biased.
- Discussion 4: parts that attack the other frameworks instead of making the case for their own. Ask for their best case first.
- Colliders are in the reading and not in this class. If a group's rival graph has one, note it and move on.
